summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, so the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. In Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Physical risk is rising. Reporting in August 2026 documents vigilante mobs attacking transgender women and ties the surge to officials' statements and to an October 2025 presidential decree of President Prabowo Subianto declaring the spread of LGBTQ culture a non-military national threat, placed alongside separatism and terrorism. An academic commentator cited by ABC News states that the regulation moves the rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy, framing LGBTQ people as risks to be monitored and controlled.

Custody risk is documented. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard graduate student and trans woman, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali. During a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release; she alleges police beat him. He died in custody, and Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's deputy director Wirya Adiwena called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

Expression is criminalised. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction penalises any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. The national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal in March 2016. The government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related terms, including Grindr, and closed the Instagram account of the comic Alpantuni; a bill explicitly prohibiting online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised on Indonesian documents, with no third gender or X option. Transgender Indonesians have gender at birth printed on identification papers unless they have obtained court recognition; legal gender can be changed after sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, after which marriage to someone of the opposite legal gender is possible. The sources do not describe how Indonesian border or airport authorities treat foreign identity documents carrying an X marker or a marker that differs from the holder's presentation.

No specific law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people. The protection machinery that exists is narrow: a police circular issued since 2015 directs the processing of hate speech related to sexual orientation and gender identity, and Regulation of the Head of National Police Number 8 of 2009 stipulates the duty to protect minority groups' special rights including sexual orientation.
tangentialFactors:
The institutional posture predates the current escalation. Human Rights Watch's report of 10 August 2016, 'These Political Games Ruin Our Lives', records the Indonesian Psychiatric Association proclaiming same-sex orientation and transgender identities mental illnesses and recommending psychological rehabilitation, while the Jokowi government remained mostly silent. That report marks the origin point of the institutionalised anti-LGBT posture on which later legal measures build.

Human Rights Watch reported on 7 July 2026 a surge in abuse against LGBT students, following officials' condemnations of a student group at Universitas Indonesia. The organisation has documented discriminatory regulations, arrests and criminal trials against LGBT people in Indonesia since 2016, and Arus Pelangi, Indonesia's LGBT umbrella organisation, documented 94 cases. In early July 2026 officials called on parents to monitor children in 'this lifestyle'.

The extra-marital sex provision is not drafted in same-sex terms; it reaches any consensual sex outside marriage. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex therefore faces that national provision together with the province-level offences where they apply, while a heterosexual visitor outside marriage faces the national provision alone. Because prosecution is reported as selective, exposure depends on complaint and locality rather than on a uniform enforcement pattern.
localsOnly:
Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with identification papers (Kartu Tanda Penduduk) across multiple provinces including Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua. Many were undocumented, especially where families disapproved, which left them without access to work or social services.

Since 2018 the Jakarta Social Agency has declared transgender women (waria) 'socially dysfunctional', regularly conducted raids against them and taken detained individuals to city-owned 'rehabilitation' centres where they are incarcerated alongside homeless people and released only after signing a promise not to repeat their 'offence'. Officials stated that the measure is meant as a deterrent against being transgender.

Conversion therapy is widely practiced and openly advertised in rehabilitation centres, including corrective rape from family members against lesbian women. LGBTQ groups are working on setting up safe houses and evacuation plans. Yayasan Srikandi Sejati provides HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers at a free health clinic, and Yogyakarta has the only madrasa for transgender people in the world.

Employment protection exists only in general form. The Constitution and Human Rights Law (No. 39/1999) theoretically guarantee protection against discriminatory employment practices on any ground. The Attorney General's Office rescinded a public job offer declaring that LGBTQ persons need not apply, after advice from the National Commission on Human Rights. A police brigadier (TT) was fired for being gay after colleagues outed him, and the Semarang State Administrative Court rejected his lawsuit in May 2019 on procedural grounds.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not describe entry, visa or airport document screening for trans visitors, including treatment of foreign passports carrying an X marker or a marker that differs from the holder's presentation. The only airport-related account in the inventory is the 2022 arrest in Bali.

Whether the 2025 bill explicitly prohibiting online content presenting LGBT behaviour has been enacted is unresolved in these sources, as is whether the extra-marital sex provision of the new penal code has been applied to foreign nationals.

Enforcement in South Sumatra is not documented beyond the province's criminalising statute; no prosecution or sentence under that statute appears in the inventory, and the same is true of the national provision outside Aceh.

No denominator-based violence data is available. The sources give no population figure or general homicide rate against which attacks on transgender people could be measured, so the magnitude of the physical risk cannot be quantified from this inventory.

Whether the October 2025 presidential decree has produced specific enforcement directives affecting foreign visitors, as distinct from domestic policy and monitoring, is not sourced.
